claim: Experience and training facilitate the ability to extract and discriminate meaningful patterns from cluttered environments.
source: Experience and training have been shown to facilitate our ability to extract and discriminate meaningful patterns from cluttered environments.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Task-dependent GABAergic inhibition in the occipito-temporal cortex relates to functional brain plasticity and behavioral improvement.
source: Our results demonstrate that task-dependent GABAergic inhibition relates to functional brain plasticity and behavioral improvement.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study combining fMRI and MRS measurements

claim: Decreased GABA in the occipito-temporal cortex relates to noise filtering during learning.
source: Specifically, GABAergic inhibition in the occipito-temporal cortex relates to dissociable learning mechanisms: decreased GABA for noise filtering, while increased GABA for feature template retuning.
evidence: Supported by MRS measurements showing correlations between GABA changes and behavioral improvement in the signal-in-noise task

claim: Increased GABA in the occipito-temporal cortex relates to feature template retuning during learning.
source: Specifically, GABAergic inhibition in the occipito-temporal cortex relates to dissociable learning mechanisms: decreased GABA for noise filtering, while increased GABA for feature template retuning.
evidence: Supported by MRS measurements showing correlations between GABA changes and behavioral improvement in the feature-differences task

claim: Perturbing cortical excitability during training with tDCs alters performance in a task-specific manner.
source: Perturbing cortical excitability during training with tDCs alters performance in a task-specific manner, providing evidence for a direct link between suppression and behavioral improvement.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from tDCs intervention showing differential effects on the two tasks

claim: fMRI alone does not allow discernment of inhibitory versus excitatory mechanisms.
source: To test the role of suppression in perceptual learning, we combine fMRI with MR Spectroscopy measurements of GABA, as fMRI alone does not allow us to discern inhibitory vs. excitatory mechanisms.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about BOLD signal limitations

claim: Theoretical models of perceptual learning posit that training facilitates the ability to detect targets in clutter by filtering external noise.
source: Theoretical models of perceptual learning (Dosher et al., 2013; Dosher and Lu, 1998; Li et al., 2004) posit that experience and training facilitate our ability to a) detect targets in clutter by filtering external noise, b) discriminate highly similar objects by suppressing irrelevant features and retuning task-relevant feature templates.
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical models

claim: Theoretical models of perceptual learning posit that training facilitates the ability to discriminate highly similar objects by suppressing irrelevant features and retuning task-relevant feature templates.
source: Theoretical models of perceptual learning (Dosher et al., 2013; Dosher and Lu, 1998; Li et al., 2004) posit that experience and training facilitate our ability to a) detect targets in clutter by filtering external noise, b) discriminate highly similar objects by suppressing irrelevant features and retuning task-relevant feature templates.
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical models

claim: BOLD reflects aggregate activity across large neural populations.
source: However, fMRI data do not allow us to discern excitatory from suppressive mechanisms of experience-dependent plasticity, as BOLD reflects aggregate activity across large neural populations (Heeger and Ress, 2002; Logothetis, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature on BOLD signal properties

claim: GABAergic inhibition in animals is associated with learning and synaptic plasticity.
source: Previous work in animals has demonstrated that GABAergic inhibition is associated with learning and synaptic plasticity (Castro-Alamancos et al., 1995; Trepel and Racine, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to animal studies

claim: GABA concentrations in the visual cortex relate to homeostatic plasticity.
source: Previous MRS studies have shown that GABA concentrations in the visual cortex relate to homeostatic plasticity (Lunghi et al., 2015), while GABA concentrations in the motor cortex relate to individual ability (Kolasinski et al., 2017; Stagg et al., 2011a) and improved performance (Blicher et al., 2015; Floyer-Lea et al., 2006; O'Shea et al., 2017; Sampaio-Baptista et al., 2015) in motor learning.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous MRS studies

claim: GABA concentrations in the motor cortex relate to individual ability in motor learning.
source: Previous MRS studies have shown that GABA concentrations in the visual cortex relate to homeostatic plasticity (Lunghi et al., 2015), while GABA concentrations in the motor cortex relate to individual ability (Kolasinski et al., 2017; Stagg et al., 2011a) and improved performance (Blicher et al., 2015; Floyer-Lea et al., 2006; O'Shea et al., 2017; Sampaio-Baptista et al., 2015) in motor learning.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous MRS studies

claim: GABA concentrations in the motor cortex relate to improved performance in motor learning.
source: Previous MRS studies have shown that GABA concentrations in the visual cortex relate to homeostatic plasticity (Lunghi et al., 2015), while GABA concentrations in the motor cortex relate to individual ability (Kolasinski et al., 2017; Stagg et al., 2011a) and improved performance (Blicher et al., 2015; Floyer-Lea et al., 2006; O'Shea et al., 2017; Sampaio-Baptista et al., 2015) in motor learning.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous MRS studies

claim: Participants improved during a single training session that took place during scanning.
source: For each task, participants improved during a single training session that took place during scanning (Figure 1b), consistent with previous reports showing fast behavioral improvement early in the training (for a review see Sagi, 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b and consistent with previous literature

claim: Performance was significantly improved after training compared to the first training run.
source: A repeated measures ANOVA (Task (SN vs. FD) x Training (training runs) showed significantly improved performance –as measured by d'– after training (main effect of Training: F(6,192)= 3.79, p=0.001) but no significant effect of Task (F(1,32)=0.01, p=0.91) nor Training x Task interaction (F(6,192)= 0.61, p=0.722), suggesting similar improvement in both tasks.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data

claim: There was no significant difference in behavioral improvement between the signal-in-noise and feature-differences tasks.
source: A repeated measures ANOVA (Task (SN vs. FD) x Training (training runs) showed significantly improved performance –as measured by d'– after training (main effect of Training: F(6,192)= 3.79, p=0.001) but no significant effect of Task (F(1,32)=0.01, p=0.91) nor Training x Task interaction (F(6,192)= 0.61, p=0.722), suggesting similar improvement in both tasks.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data

claim: Performance improvement due to training was lasting, as shown by testing participants the day after training.
source: Testing participants the following day after training (transfer test) showed that performance was significantly different from the first training run for both tasks (main effect of Session: (F(1,32)= 10.59, p=0.003; Task x Session interaction: (F(1,32)=0.89, p=0.35) but not significantly different from the last training run (main effect of Session: F(1,32)=0.95, p=0.34; Task x Session interaction: F(1,32)=0.18, p=0.68), suggesting lasting performance improvement due to training.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from transfer test

claim: No significant changes in performance were observed for a no-training control group who did not receive training between test sessions.
source: In contrast, no significant changes in performance were observed for a no-training control group who did not receive training in between test sessions (main effect of Session: F(1,6)= 1.13, p=0.33; Task x Session interaction: F(1,6)=0.0003, p=0.99) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of control group data

claim: BOLD change in the posterior occipito-temporal cortex correlates with behavioral improvement across tasks.
source: Our results showed significant correlations between BOLD change (late vs. early training runs) in the posterior occipito-temporal cortex and behavioral improvement (learning rate, Δd') across tasks (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by whole-brain covariance analysis of fMRI data

claim: The posterior occipito-temporal cortex is involved in visual learning and global shape processing.
source: These results provide evidence for learning-dependent changes in occipito-temporal cortex that relate to behavioral improvement, consistent with our previous studies and the role of this region in visual learning and global shape processing (Kourtzi et al., 2005; Kuai et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by current data and citations to previous studies

claim: For the Signal-in-noise task, GABA change correlated negatively with learning rate.
source: In particular, for the Signal-in-noise task we observed a negative correlation of GABA change with learning rate (r = −0.43, CI=[−0.74,–0.07]), but no significant correlation with Δd' (r = −0.14, CI=[−0.49, 0.29]).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of MRS and behavioral data

claim: For the Feature-differences task, GABA change correlated positively with Δd'.
source: In contrast, for the Feature-differences, task we observed a positive correlation of GABA change with Δd' (r = 0.54, CI=[0.05, 0.85]), but no significant correlation with learning rate (r = 0.13, CI=[−0.38, 0.62]).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of MRS and behavioral data

claim: The correlations of GABA change with behavioral improvement were significantly different between the two tasks.
source: Further, the significant correlations of GABA change with behavioral improvement (learning rate for SN; Δd' for FD) were significantly different between tasks (Fisher's z = 2.91, p=0.004).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of correlations between tasks

claim: The dissociable effects of GABA change on behavioral improvement could not be explained by differences in overall performance between tasks.
source: These dissociable effects could not be simply explained by differences in overall performance between tasks, as the two tasks resulted in similar behavioral improvement.
evidence: Based on inference from the similar behavioral improvement observed in both tasks

claim: No significant differences were observed in mean GABA concentration in occipito-temporal cortex before versus after training.
source: We did not observe significant differences in mean GABA concentration in occipito-temporal cortex before vs. after training (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of MRS data

claim: Correlation of GABA change and behavioral improvement remained significant when correcting for tissue composition.
source: First, correlation of GABA change and behavioral improvement remained significant when we corrected for a) tissue (grey matter, white matter, cerebrospinal fluid) composition (SN, correlation with learning rate: r = −0.41, CI=[−0.70,–0.07]; FD, correlation with Δd': r = 0.56, CI=[0.03, 0.83]) and b) differences in data quality (as measured by Cramer-Rao Lower Bounds – see Materials and methods) between the two GABA measurements (SN, correlation with learning rate: r = −0.44, CI=[−0.71,–0.12]; FD, correlation with Δd': r = 0.46, CI=[0.03, 0.76]).
evidence: Supported by control analyses of MRS data

claim: Changes in Glutamate did not correlate significantly with behavioral improvement.
source: Third, changes in Glutamate, the other major cortical neurotransmitter, did not correlate significantly with behavioral improvement (SN, correlation of Glutamate change with learning rate: r = 0.33, CI=[−0.22, 0.67]; FD, correlation of Glutamate change with Δd': r = −0.30, CI=[−0.58, 0.06]).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of MRS glutamate measurements

claim: The findings were specific to GABA and do not generalize to glutamate.
source: Further, correlations of GABA change and behavioral improvement remained significant after accounting for Glutamate change (SN, correlation of GABA change with learning rate: r = −0.41, CI=[−0.69,–0.08]; FD, correlation of GABA change with Δd': r = 0.54, CI=[0.04, 0.85]), suggesting that our results were specific to GABA and do not generalize to glutamate.
evidence: Supported by control analyses accounting for glutamate

claim: Learning-related GABA changes are specific to occipito-temporal cortex rather than reflecting changes in global cortical excitability.
source: We did not find significant correlations between posterior parietal GABA change and behavioral improvement for either task (SN: r = −0.23, CI=[−0.61, 0.19]; FD: r = 0.05, CI=[−0.37, 0.43]), suggesting that our findings are specific to local changes in occipito-temporal GABA rather than reflecting changes in global cortical excitability.
evidence: Supported by control measurements in posterior parietal cortex

claim: GABA change correlated negatively with BOLD change for the Signal-in-Noise task.
source: This analysis showed opposite correlations between GABA and BOLD change for the two tasks: negative correlation for the Signal-in-Noise, while positive correlation for the Feature-differences task (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by GLM covariance analysis of fMRI and MRS data

claim: GABA change correlated positively with BOLD change for the Feature-differences task.
source: This analysis showed opposite correlations between GABA and BOLD change for the two tasks: negative correlation for the Signal-in-Noise, while positive correlation for the Feature-differences task (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by GLM covariance analysis of fMRI and MRS data

claim: Correlations of change in GABA and BOLD extracted from an independently defined region of interest were opposite and significantly different between the two tasks.
source: Correlations of change in GABA and BOLD –extracted from this independently defined region of interest (Figure 1c)- were opposite and significantly different between the two tasks (SN: r = −0.58 CI=[−0.82,–0.22], FD: r = 0.70 CI=[0.37, 0.90], Fisher's z = 4.19, p<0.0001) (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis using independently defined ROI

claim: Task-dependent GABAergic inhibition moderates the relationship between functional brain plasticity and behavioral improvement in the visual cortex.
source: These results suggest that task-dependent GABAergic inhibition moderates the relationship between functional brain plasticity and behavioral improvement in the visual cortex.
evidence: Supported by moderation analysis showing significant three-way interaction

claim: There were no significant differences in GABA concentration before training between the two groups.
source: First, our analyses did not show any significant differences in GABA concentration before training (t(34)=0.11, p=0.91) nor in behavioral performance early in training (i.e. first training run) (t(34)=0.23, p=0.82) between the two groups.
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison between groups

claim: There were no significant differences in behavioral performance early in training between the two groups.
source: First, our analyses did not show any significant differences in GABA concentration before training (t(34)=0.11, p=0.91) nor in behavioral performance early in training (i.e. first training run) (t(34)=0.23, p=0.82) between the two groups.
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison between groups

claim: There were no significant differences in MRS signal-to-noise ratio between the two tasks.
source: We did not find any significant differences in MRS SNR (t(34)=0.77, p=0.45), nor fMRI temporal SNR (tSNR) between the two tasks (t(34)=0.73, p=0.47).
evidence: Supported by comparison of data quality metrics between tasks

claim: Anodal tDCs is excitatory and has been shown to result in local GABA reduction in visual cortex.
source: In particular, anodal tDCs is known to be excitatory (Nitsche and Paulus, 2000) and has been shown to result in local GABA reduction in visual (Barron et al., 2016) and motor cortex (Stagg et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous tDCs studies

claim: Anodal tDCs has been shown to facilitate learning in motor and perceptual tasks.
source: Further, anodal tDCs has been shown to facilitate learning in motor (O'Shea et al., 2017; Stagg et al., 2011c) and perceptual tasks (Fertonani et al., 2011; Pirulli et al., 2013; Sczesny-Kaiser et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous tDCs studies

claim: Cathodal stimulation is inhibitory and has been shown to reduce cortical excitability.
source: In contrast, cathodal stimulation is thought to be inhibitory; that is, it has been shown to reduce cortical excitability (Nitsche and Paulus, 2000) by decreasing glutamatergic transmission (Stagg et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous tDCs studies

claim: Cathodal tDCs on the occipital cortex has been shown to facilitate performance in perceptual judgments by suppressing incorrect sensory input.
source: Further, cathodal tDCs on the occipital cortex has been shown to facilitate performance in perceptual judgments by suppressing incorrect sensory input (Antal et al., 2004b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous tDCs study

claim: Performance was significantly improved for anodal compared to sham stimulation for the Signal-in-Noise task.
source: Our results (Figure 4) showed significant improvement in behavioral performance, as measured by d', for anodal compared to sham stimulation for the Signal-in-Noise (Training block x Stimulation: F(2,52.5) = 3.99, p=0.02) but not the Feature-differences task (Training block x Stimulation: F(2.2,57.9) = 0.45, p=0.66).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of tDCs behavioral data

claim: Performance was improved during cathodal compared to sham tDCs for the Feature-differences task.
source: In contrast, we observed improved performance during cathodal compared to sham tDCs for the Feature-differences task (main effect of Stimulation: F(1,26)= 6.13, p=0.02) but not the Signal-in-Noise task (main effect of Stimulation: F(1,26)= 0.001, p=0.98).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of tDCs behavioral data

claim: There was a significant Task, Stimulation x Training block interaction for performance normalized to sham stimulation.
source: A repeated-measures ANOVA showed a significant Task, Stimulation x Training block interaction (F(2.5, 130)=3.19, p=0.03).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of normalized tDCs behavioral data

claim: The tDCs-induced learning effects were not due to differences in difficulty across tasks.
source: Comparing performance across participants before training (i.e. pre-training block with no feedback or stimulation) showed no significant effect of Task (F(1,78)=0.05, p=0.82), nor a significant interaction between Task and Stimulation group (F(2,78)=0.92, p=0.40), suggesting that the tDCs-induced learning effects were not due to differences in difficulty across tasks (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by control analysis of pre-training performance

claim: All participants including the sham stimulation groups were able to learn the task.
source: This was further supported by a significant main effect of Session (F(1,78)=86.99, p<0.0001) across stimulation groups suggesting that all participants (including the sham stimulation groups) were able to learn the task (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing main effect of session

claim: Comparing performance on consecutive days in a no-training control group showed no significant improvement.
source: In contrast, comparing performance on consecutive days in a no-training control group (participants were tested twice but without training on the task) showed no significant main effect of Session (F(1,17)= 0.78, p=0.39) nor a significant interaction between Task and Session (F(1,17)=0.30, p=0.59), suggesting that the learning effects we observed were training-specific.
evidence: Supported by control group data showing no improvement without training

claim: Improved performance was maintained across all groups when participants were tested without tDCs stimulation.
source: A repeated-measures ANOVA showed no significant interaction between Session x Stimulation x Task (F(2,78)=1.09, p=0.34), suggesting that improved performance was maintained across all groups when participants were tested without tDCs stimulation.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of post-training test data

claim: GABAergic inhibition in the visual cortex underlies dissociable learning mechanisms that optimize the ability to make perceptual decisions.
source: Our findings propose that GABAergic inhibition in the visual cortex underlies dissociable learning mechanisms that optimize our ability to make perceptual decisions.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined results of MRS, fMRI, and tDCs experiments

claim: Excitatory anodal stimulation enhances learning to see in clutter.
source: In particular, we demonstrate that excitatory stimulation enhances performance during training to detect targets from noise, while inhibitory stimulation enhances fine feature discriminability.
evidence: Supported by tDCs experimental results

claim: Inhibitory cathodal stimulation enhances learning of fine feature differences.
source: In particular, we demonstrate that excitatory stimulation enhances performance during training to detect targets from noise, while inhibitory stimulation enhances fine feature discriminability.
evidence: Supported by tDCs experimental results

claim: GABAergic processing in visual cortex optimizes noise filtering for target detection.
source: Taken together, our findings suggest that GABAergic processing in visual cortex optimizes noise filtering for target detection, while retuning of feature templates for fine discrimination.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined experimental results

claim: GABAergic processing in visual cortex optimizes retuning of feature templates for fine discrimination.
source: Taken together, our findings suggest that GABAergic processing in visual cortex optimizes noise filtering for target detection, while retuning of feature templates for fine discrimination.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined experimental results

claim: Interrogating fMRI signals alone does not allow discernment between the brain mechanisms that underlie learning to detect targets in clutter versus discriminating similar features.
source: Interrogating fMRI signals alone does not allow us to discern between the brain mechanisms that underlie these skills, as BOLD reflects the aggregate activity of excitatory and inhibitory signals at the scale of large neural populations (Heeger and Ress, 2002; Logothetis, 2008).
evidence: Based on established knowledge about BOLD signal limitations and supported by citations

claim: The results showed similar learning dependent changes in behavioral performance and BOLD in the two tasks at early stages of learning.
source: Our results showed similar learning dependent changes in behavioral performance and BOLD in these tasks at early stages of learning (i.e. training for a single session).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study

claim: Previous fMRI studies of perceptual learning have shown learning-dependent changes in the overall fMRI responses in visual cortex.
source: This is consistent with previous fMRI studies of perceptual learning that have shown learning-dependent changes in the overall fMRI responses in visual cortex (e.g. [Kourtzi et al., 2005; Mukai et al., 2007; Sigman et al., 2005]), or enhanced discriminability of fMRI patterns with training (Byers and Serences, 2014; Jehee et al., 2012; Kuai et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous fMRI studies

claim: Combining MRS measurements of GABA with fMRI uncovers distinct suppression mechanisms that moderate the relationship between behavioral improvement and experience-dependent plasticity in visual cortex.
source: However, combining MRS measurements of GABA with fMRI uncovers distinct suppression mechanisms that moderate the relationship between behavioral improvement and experience-dependent plasticity in visual cortex.
evidence: Supported by the combined MRS and fMRI experimental results

claim: Previous studies have investigated the relationship of baseline GABA measurements with performance in visual and sensory-motor tasks.
source: Previous studies have investigated the relationship of baseline GABA measurements with performance in the context of visual (Edden et al., 2009) and sensory-motor tasks (Heba et al., 2016; Kolasinski et al., 2017; Stagg et al., 2011a) as well as reward-based learning (Scholl et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Previous studies have reported changes in GABA within the range and time scales observed in this study due to stimulation or training.
source: Previous studies have reported changes in GABA within the range and time scales observed in our study (10–15% change observed within 20–30 min) due to stimulation (Barron et al., 2016; O'Shea et al., 2017; Stagg et al., 2009) or training (Floyer-Lea et al., 2006) suggesting a role for GABAergic inhibition across stages of learning (Sampaio-Baptista et al., 2015; Shibata et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: MRS-measured GABA reflects primarily extra-synaptic GABA concentrations.
source: Although, the precise mechanisms that underlie changes in GABA as measured by MRS are still under investigation (Stagg, 2014), recent animal (Mason et al., 2001) and human (Stagg et al., 2011b) studies suggest that MRS-measured GABA reflects primarily extra-synaptic GABA concentrations.
evidence: Supported by citations to animal and human studies

claim: For learning to see in clutter, decreased occipito-temporal GABA relates to increased BOLD and improved performance.
source: In particular, for learning to see in clutter, decreased occipito-temporal GABA relates to increased BOLD and improved performance, as indicated by faster learning rate.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing correlations between GABA, BOLD, and behavior

claim: Learning to see in clutter involves enhanced noise filtering through gain control mediated by learning-dependent changes in visual cortex suppression.
source: These findings suggest enhanced noise filtering through gain control that is mediated by learning-dependent changes in visual cortex suppression.
evidence: Based on inference from the experimental results and theoretical framework

claim: GABAergic inhibition is linked to neural gain.
source: This mechanism is consistent with previous animal work linking GABAergic inhibition to neural gain (Mitchell and Silver, 2003) and interventional studies showing that blocking GABAergic inhibition increases neural gain (Hamann et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous animal and interventional studies

claim: Learning to detect targets in clutter may be implemented by decreased local suppression that facilitates recurrent processing for noise filtering and target detection.
source: It is possible that learning to detect targets in clutter is implemented by decreased local suppression that facilitates recurrent processing for noise filtering and target detection (Gilbert and Li, 2012; Poort et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations to relevant studies

claim: For learning to discriminate fine feature differences, increased occipito-temporal GABA relates to increased BOLD and improved performance.
source: In contrast, we demonstrate that for learning to discriminate fine feature differences, increased occipito-temporal GABA relates to increased BOLD and improved performance, as indicated by enhanced sensitivity in visual discrimination after training.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing correlations between GABA, BOLD, and behavior

claim: Learning to discriminate fine feature differences involves neural tuning to fine feature differences mediated by increased visual cortex suppression.
source: This finding suggests that learning to discriminate between highly similar targets by template retuning involves neural tuning to fine feature differences (Raiguel et al., 2006; Schoups et al., 2001; Yang and Maunsell, 2004) that is mediated by increased visual cortex suppression.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results and supported by citations

claim: GABAergic inhibition is linked to cortical tuning.
source: This mechanism is consistent with studies linking GABAergic inhibition to cortical tuning (Rokem et al., 2011; Wehr and Zador, 2003) and pharmacological interventions showing that GABA agonists enhance orientation selectivity in visual cortex (Leventhal et al., 2003; Li et al., 2008), while blocking GABAergic inhibition results in broader neural tuning (Leventhal et al., 2003; Sillito, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on GABAergic inhibition and cortical tuning

claim: Somatostatin-positive (SOM) interneurons have been implicated in spatial summation.
source: In particular somatostatin-positive (SOM) interneurons have been implicated in spatial summation (Adesnik et al., 2012) and have been shown to gate plasticity during training by providing contextual information (van Versendaal and Levelt, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on SOM interneurons

claim: Parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons have been implicated in selective inhibition that sharpens feature representations after training.
source: In contrast, parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons have been implicated in selective inhibition (Rokem et al., 2011) that sharpens feature representations after training (Khan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on PV interneurons

claim: The dissociable correlations between tasks for GABA change and behavioral improvement may reflect differential involvement of SOM versus PV interneurons in the two tasks.
source: It is therefore possible, that the dissociable correlations we observed between tasks for GABA change and behavioral improvement may reflect differential involvement of SOM vs. PV interneurons in the two tasks.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on inference from the results and knowledge of interneuron function

claim: SOM interneurons involved in spatial integration may support learning to detect targets from clutter through noise filtering.
source: Specifically, SOM interneurons involved in spatial integration may support learning to detect targets from clutter (SN task) through noise filtering.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on inference from the results and knowledge of SOM interneuron function

claim: PV interneurons involved in selective inhibition may support learning fine differences through re-tuning of feature templates.
source: In contrast, PV interneurons involved in selective inhibition may support learning fine differences (FD task) through re-tuning of feature templates.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on inference from the results and knowledge of PV interneuron function

claim: SOM versus PV interneurons are involved at different stages during the time course of learning.
source: Further, SOM vs. PV interneurons are shown to be involved at different stages during the time course of learning. In particular, SOM cells have been shown to gate learning-dependent plasticity during training (Chen et al., 2015), while PV cells form stimulus-specific ensembles with pyramidal cells after training on a visual discrimination task (Khan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on interneuron involvement in learning

claim: Different behavioral measures may capture the function of SOM versus PV interneurons.
source: Thus, it is possible that different behavioral measures capture the function of SOM vs. PV interneurons, consistent with the dissociation we observed between tasks for the correlations of GABA change and behavioral improvement.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on inference from the results

claim: Learning rate may capture best the function of SOM interneurons that act during learning to support noise filtering throughout the course of training.
source: In particular, learning rate (i.e. the rate with which perceptual sensitivity changes during training) may capture best the function of SOM interneurons that act during learning to support noise filtering throughout the course of training.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on inference from the results and knowledge of SOM interneuron function

claim: Δd' may capture best the function of PV interneurons that support tuning of stimulus-specific representations after training.
source: In contrast, Δd' (i.e. change in perceptual sensitivity after training) may capture best the function of PV interneurons that are shown to support tuning of stimulus-specific representations after training.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on inference from the results and knowledge of PV interneuron function

claim: The results demonstrate a double dissociation in learning-dependent mechanisms of visual plasticity.
source: Our results demonstrate a double dissociation in learning-dependent mechanisms of visual plasticity.
evidence: Supported by tDCs experimental results showing opposite effects for the two tasks

claim: Excitatory anodal stimulation enhanced learning to detect targets in clutter, consistent with the negative correlation between GABA change and behavior.
source: Excitatory anodal (rather than cathodal) stimulation enhanced learning to detect targets in clutter, consistent with the negative correlation between GABA change and behavior .
evidence: Supported by tDCs experimental results and their consistency with MRS findings

claim: Inhibitory cathodal stimulation enhanced learning to discriminate fine features, consistent with the positive correlation between GABA change and behavior.
source: In contrast, inhibitory cathodal (rather than anodal) stimulation enhanced learning to discriminate fine features, consistent with the positive correlation between GABA change and behavior .
evidence: Supported by tDCs experimental results and their consistency with MRS findings

claim: The findings demonstrate a direct link between GABAergic processing in visual cortex and enhanced visual learning.
source: These findings demonstrate a direct link between GABAergic processing in visual cortex and enhanced visual learning.
evidence: Based on inference from the combined tDCs and MRS results

claim: The findings provide novel evidence for the role of GABAergic processing in learning.
source: In sum, our findings provide novel evidence for the role of GABAergic processing in learning, shedding light on the neural implementation of theoretical models of perceptual learning.
evidence: Based on the overall experimental findings of the study

claim: The findings shed light on the neural implementation of theoretical models of perceptual learning.
source: In sum, our findings provide novel evidence for the role of GABAergic processing in learning, shedding light on the neural implementation of theoretical models of perceptual learning.
evidence: Based on the overall experimental findings and their relation to theoretical models

claim: Distinct interneuron types may differentially contribute to learning by noise filtering versus feature template retuning by changing the gain versus feature selectivity of pyramidal cells.
source: These distinct interneuron types may differentially contribute to learning by noise filtering vs. feature template retuning by changing the gain vs. feature selectivity of pyramidal cells.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on inference from the results and knowledge of interneuron function

claim: The findings propose testable hypotheses linking theoretical models of perceptual learning to the micro-circuits that mediate adaptive behavior.
source: Thus, our findings propose testable hypotheses linking theoretical models of perceptual learning to the micro-circuits that mediate adaptive behavior and underlie the macroscopic learning-dependent plasticity, as measured by human brain imaging.
evidence: Based on inference from the overall findings and their implications

claim: A hundred and thirty participants took part in this study.
source: A hundred and thirty participants took part in this study.
evidence: Direct statement of participant numbers

claim: Forty six participants participated in the brain imaging experiment.
source: Forty six participants (21 female; mean age 25.04 ± 3.69 years) participated in the brain imaging experiment and eighty four participants (45 female; mean age 23.8 ± 3.41 years) participated in the brain stimulation experiment.
evidence: Direct statement of participant numbers for brain imaging experiment

claim: Eighty four participants participated in the brain stimulation experiment.
source: Forty six participants (21 female; mean age 25.04 ± 3.69 years) participated in the brain imaging experiment and eighty four participants (45 female; mean age 23.8 ± 3.41 years) participated in the brain stimulation experiment.
evidence: Direct statement of participant numbers for brain stimulation experiment

claim: Two separate groups of participants were trained on different tasks to avoid transfer effects across tasks.
source: For the brain imaging experiment, we trained two separate groups of participants. Each group was trained only on one of the two tasks (SN, FD) to avoid transfer effects across tasks that have been previously reported when the same individuals were trained sequentially on both tasks (Chang et al., 2013; Dosher and Lu, 2007).
evidence: Methodological decision supported by citations to previous studies showing transfer effects

claim: Data from three participants were excluded from the brain imaging study due to technical failure during data acquisition.
source: Data from three participants were excluded from the study due to technical failure during data acquisition resulting in twenty one participants in the Signal-in-Noise experiment and twenty two participants in the Feature-differences experiment.
evidence: Direct statement of data exclusion

claim: Glass patterns were generated by placing dipoles orthogonally or tangentially to the circumference of a circle centered on the fixation dot.
source: We generated radial (0o spiral angle) and concentric (90o spiral angle) Glass patterns by placing dipoles orthogonally (radial stimuli) or tangentially (concentric stimuli) to the circumference of a circle centered on the fixation dot.
evidence: Direct description of stimulus generation method

claim: For the Signal-in-Noise task, radial and concentric stimuli were presented at 24 ± 1% signal level.
source: For the Signal-in-Noise task, radial and concentric stimuli (spiral angle: 0° +- 90°) were presented at 24 ± 1% signal level; that is, 76% of the dipoles were presented at random position and orientation.
evidence: Direct description of stimulus parameters

claim: For the Feature-differences task, stimuli were presented at 100% signal and spiral angle of ±38° (radial) or ±52° (concentric).
source: For the Feature-differences task, stimuli were presented at 100% signal and spiral angle of ±38o (radial) or ±52o (concentric) (Figure 1a).
evidence: Direct description of stimulus parameters

claim: MRS measurements were recorded before and after training within a voxel centered on the posterior-occipito-temporal cortex.
source: We recorded GABA concentrations before and after training within a voxel centered on the posterior-occipito-temporal cortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), consistent with the fMRI analysis showing learning-dependent BOLD changes with training in this region.
evidence: Direct description of MRS measurement procedure

claim: A 2D 1H J-PRESS sequence was used for MRS measurements.
source: We used a 2D 1H J-PRESS sequence (Prescot and Renshaw, 2013; Schulte and Boesiger, 2006) (TR/TE = 2000/31–229 ms; ΔTE = 2 ms (100 TE steps); four signal averages per TE step with online averaging; 2D spectral width = 2000×500 Hz, and 2D matrix size = 1024×100).
evidence: Direct description of MRS acquisition parameters with citations

claim: Measurements with the 2D 1H J-PRESS sequence at 3T have been previously shown to be reliable and reproducible.
source: Measurements with this sequence at 3T have been previously shown to be reliable and reproducible (Prescot and Renshaw, 2013; Schmitz et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous validation studies

claim: 1mA current was delivered for 35 minutes in the anodal and cathodal tDCs conditions.
source: In the anodal and cathodal conditions, 1mA current was ramped up over 10 s, was held at 1mA for 35 min and was subsequently ramped down over 10 s.
evidence: Direct description of tDCs stimulation parameters

claim: Online stimulation during training has been previously shown to enhance the lasting effect of training.
source: We used online stimulation (i.e. stimulation during training), as this protocol has been previously shown to enhance the lasting effect of training (O'Shea et al., 2017).
evidence: Methodological decision supported by citation to previous study

claim: d' was computed as the difference between the z-transform of each stimulus class' hit and false alarm rates.
source: To quantify discriminability between the two Glass patterns classes (radial vs. concentric), we computed d' (Stanislaw and Todorov, 1999) across trials per run, as the difference between the z-transform of each stimulus class' hit and false alarm rates.
evidence: Direct description of behavioral analysis method with citation

claim: MRS data were pre-processed using MATLAB and the prior-knowledge fitting software ProFit.
source: We pre-processed MRS data according to (Prescot and Renshaw, 2013), using MATLAB 2013a (The MathWorks, Natick, MA, USA) and the prior-knowledge fitting software ProFit (Schulte and Boesiger, 2006).
evidence: Direct description of MRS data processing methods with citations

claim: Only participant data without contamination and GABA CRLB values < 20% for both pre- and post-training fitted data were included in MRS analyses.
source: Only participant data without contamination (e.g. due to lipids) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and GABA CRLB values < 20% for both pre- and post-training fitted data were included in further steps of MRS related analyses (data from three participants for the Feature-differences task were excluded based on these criteria).
evidence: Direct description of data quality criteria for inclusion

claim: Metabolite concentrations were referenced to the concentration of total Creatine.
source: We referenced metabolite concentrations to the concentration of total Creatine (tCre). tCre has been widely used as a reference metabolite in MRS studies (Donahue et al., 2010; Sampaio-Baptista et al., 2015) and this referencing method has been shown to have better reproducibility compared to other methods (Bogner et al., 2010).
evidence: Methodological decision supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Bootstrapped Pearson's correlations were used to measure the linear association between variables.
source: We used bootstrapped Pearson's correlations to measure the linear association between variables (GABA, behavioral improvement, BOLD change) as implemented in the Robust Correlation toolbox (Pernet et al., 2012).
evidence: Direct description of statistical method with citation

claim: BrainVoyager QX 2.8 was used for fMRI data analysis.
source: We used BrainVoyager QX 2.8 (Brain Innovation, Maastricht, The Netherlands) for fMRI data analysis (Goebel et al., 2006).
evidence: Direct description of software used for fMRI analysis

claim: Three participants with excessive motion across experimental runs were excluded from fMRI related analyses.
source: Three participants with excessive motion across experimental runs were excluded from fMRI related analyses (one for the Feature-differences task and two for the Signal-in-Noise task).
evidence: Direct statement of data exclusion criteria
